paragraphs: Decision center: the work of a dietetic technician is to turn a patient's food intake, weight change and dietary history into a nutrition care chain that is verifiable, handover-ready and usable under the supervision of a dietitian — first observing and recording intake and weight according to procedure, then collecting dietary history and assisting with nutrition screening and assessment, then preparing and distributing meals according to established guidelines and therapeutic diet requirements, and finally reporting changes, progress and dietary problems to the dietitian truthfully and keeping records. The focus of judgment is not whether you can cook, but whether every step along the chain of observation and recording — collection and screening — preparation and issuing — reporting and handover has a basis and is traceable, so that dietitians, nursing staff and catering colleagues can all review it.

Worth trying first: you are willing to record item by item according to procedure rather than judging from impressions, can stay careful in repetitive recording and verification work, are willing to communicate repeatedly with patients, families, nursing and catering staff and to make yourself understood, can accept the institution's hygiene, sample retention, disinfection and infection control requirements, and clearly know which judgments must be left to the dietitian or physician rather than concluding yourself.

Requires caution: if you do not want to do repetitive recording and verification, tend to give patients advice on what to eat based on experience, or find it hard to accept hard requirements such as disinfection, sample retention and wearing protective equipment, or expect to give nutrition diagnoses and treatment prescriptions directly, then the actual work experience usually does not match expectations.

Low-risk verification: use a fictional inpatient's food intake record and weight change table to complete an exercise in marking the changes that must be reported to the dietitian according to given rules, organising a set of key points from the dietary history, writing a handover record for the dietitian, and listing the items in this check that are uncertain and need to be raised; this only verifies whether you are willing to check item by item according to procedure and hand over truthfully. The exercise uses fictional material, does not touch any real patient information, does not give a nutrition diagnosis or meal prescription, and does not equal completed training, practice qualification or industry certification.

Decision center: whether how much the patient ate, how the weight changed and which points in the dietary history need attention can be organised into a care and handover chain that the dietitian can understand, that nursing and catering colleagues can continue, and that leaves a trace in the records.

The work is mainly in controlled indoor settings with extensive contact with people: indoors in a controlled environment 91% every day, continuous contact with others 78%, face-to-face discussion 79% every day, telephone conversation 58% every day; exposure to disease or infection 82% every day, exposure to distracting or uncomfortable noise 66% every day, wearing common protective or safety equipment 65% every day; work in a team is extremely important 72%, dealing with external customers or the public extremely important 59%, coordinating or leading others extremely important 58%; the importance of precision or accuracy is extremely important 57%, time pressure 61% every day, and very high responsibility for the health and safety of other employees 71%. Workplaces are hospital wards, nutrition departments and catering rooms, long-term care and rehabilitation facilities, and schools and group catering units, and the pace is determined by patient mealtimes, catering shifts and ward rounds and meeting schedules.

Similar names do not mean the same duties: this page is O*NET-SOC 29-2051.00 Dietetic Technicians, whose core is assisting with food service and nutrition programmes under the supervision of a registered dietitian. Adjacent positions have different duties — dietitians and nutritionists are responsible for nutrition diagnosis, nutrition therapy and the recommendations and prescriptions of medical nutrition therapy (this occupation carries them out under their supervision), food service managers are responsible for operations and staff and cost management, cooks and catering staff are responsible for bulk production and serving, and nursing assistants are responsible for daily patient care and some feeding assistance. The specific authorization is governed by the institution's rules, the job description and local regulations, is not inferred from the job title, and nutrition diagnosis or meal prescriptions must not be undertaken independently.

Inputs that must be verified: records of the patient's food intake and eating method, changes in indicators such as weight and fluid balance, dietary history and restrictions such as allergies and swallowing and chewing difficulties, the medical order or dietitian's requirements for therapeutic diets and food for special medical purposes, the meal-by-meal and portion calculation against the menu, and records for food ingredients, sample retention, tableware disinfection and infection control. What must not be done: do not give a nutrition diagnosis or treatment plan on your own, do not change an ordered diet or portion without authorization, do not promise treatment outcomes to patients or families, do not omit sample retention, disinfection and temperature verification records, do not use a patient's dietary and weight information for purposes other than care, and do not carry out specialised procedures such as enteral nutrition preparation without training.

Fit judgments should be made in combination with whether records and verification can be done item by item according to procedure, whether care is maintained in repetitive work, whether spoken information can be turned into accurate written records, whether restraint is maintained amid patients' and families' emotions and urgency, and whether one's own boundaries of responsibility are clear, and should not be replaced by a self-assessment of liking to cook or knowing a bit about nutrition; these all need to be confirmed in supervised practical placement and work.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional material; real nutrition screening and assessment, enteral nutrition preparation, medical diet arrangement and therapeutic diet adjustment must be carried out by trained and authorized nutrition technical personnel according to institutional rules, and nutrition diagnosis and treatment must be undertaken by physicians trained in clinical nutrition (for example, in mainland China according to the Guidelines for the Construction and Management of Clinical Nutrition Departments (trial)). Individuals must not carry out diagnosis, treatment or prescription interventions on their own, and this page does not constitute medical, compliance or legal advice.

The object of this occupation's work is a person's food intake and nutritional status and the steps that carry it out: records of intake and eating method, changes in weight and related indicators, dietary history and food allergies and swallowing restrictions, the arrangement and distribution of therapeutic diets and special meals, records for food ingredients, sample retention and disinfection, and the content reported to the dietitian and taught to patients; the outputs are intake and weight monitoring records, material assisting nutrition screening and assessment, menu and recipe and portion calculation tables, therapeutic diet arrangement and issuing records, and teaching and meeting records; the basis for judgment is established guidelines, the dietitian's requirements and institutional rules and food safety and infection control provisions, not personal experience or job title.

Judgment one: whether observation and recording are complete — whether intake and eating method are recorded truthfully by meal, and whether weight and related indicators are measured and registered according to procedure, rather than filled in from impressions.

Judgment two: whether changes requiring reporting are identified — whether a marked drop in intake, short-term weight change, repeated leftovers or refusal to eat, and symptoms possibly related to diet are reported to the dietitian or nursing staff promptly according to established rules.

Judgment three: whether dietary history and restriction information is fully verified — whether allergies, swallowing and chewing difficulties, religious and cultural dietary requirements and the ordered diet category are verified item by item and turned into executable catering requirements.

Judgment four: whether preparation and issuing leave a trace according to procedure — whether the arrangement, portion, temperature and recipients of therapeutic diets and special meals are verified against the sheet, and whether sample retention, tableware disinfection and food ingredient records are complete.

Judgment five: whether teaching and communication stay within the scope of authorization — what is explained to patients and families is the plan determined by the dietitian and general dietary principles, not treatment advice given on one's own; when uncertain, ask first.

Judgment six: whether collaboration and handover are clear — when handing over to dietitians, nursing, catering and the clinical team, whether what has been done, what has not been done and what is to be confirmed are written clearly, so that the next colleague can continue.

Environment and pace: mainly in a controlled indoor environment (91% every day), with workplaces including wards, nutrition departments and catering rooms; continuous contact with others 78%, face-to-face discussion 79% every day, telephone conversation 58% every day; exposure to disease or infection 82% and noise 66% every day, wearing common protective or safety equipment 65% every day; time pressure 61% every day, the importance of precision or accuracy extremely important 57%, and very high responsibility for the health and safety of other employees 71%.

The principle for choosing adjacent positions is that they are easily confused within the same nutrition and catering system, or have a job rotation or transfer relationship with this occupation. The purpose of the comparison is not to rank them but to explain their respective duty boundaries and scopes of authorization — in particular, nutrition diagnosis and prescribing authority cannot be borne by an execution position.

The basis for choice can follow three clues: if you want to face patients and families directly and are willing to record and execute under a dietitian's supervision, this occupation is the closest; if you want to take on nutrition assessment, diagnosis and the formulation of treatment plans, you need the dietitian and nutritionist path and must meet its education, internship and examination conditions; if you prefer kitchen output and the catering rhythm, institutional and cafeteria cooks are more suitable; if you want operations, cost and staff management, food service manager is another path. Dietitians and nutritionists (29-1031.00)

Conduct nutrition assessment and diagnosis, formulate and adjust nutrition therapy plans and medical nutrition therapy recommendations, determine the use of therapeutic diets and food for special medical purposes, run nutrition clinics and consultations and supervise the execution steps.

The level of authorization differs: dietitians are responsible for nutrition assessment, diagnosis and treatment plans and may recommend or prescribe enteral and parenteral nutrition and food for special medical purposes; this occupation executes monitoring, recording, screening assistance, meal arrangement and teaching under their supervision and is not responsible for diagnosis and plans. The mainland China scope likewise assigns nutrition diagnosis and treatment to physicians trained in clinical nutrition, while nutrition technical personnel carry out consultation, screening and assessment, enteral nutrition preparation, medical diet arrangement and teaching.

If the goal is to formulate nutrition therapy plans and bear diagnostic responsibility, you should take the dietitian and nutritionist path and verify the education, internship and examination conditions (the United States registered dietitian direction has separate education and internship requirements); if you want to enter the nutrition care setting sooner and start with execution and recording, this occupation is closer. When transferring, clinical nutrition knowledge, use of assessment tools and plan-writing capability need to be built up.
Institutional and cafeteria cooks (35-2012.00)

Complete bulk ingredient preparation and cooking according to the menu and portions, control output quality and serving times, implement kitchen hygiene and operating standards, and ensure that serving is not interrupted during peak periods.

The focus differs: cooks are responsible for production technique, taste and the serving rhythm; this occupation is responsible for arrangement and verification against the ordered category and nutrition requirements, intake and weight records, and sample retention, disinfection and ingredient files. A cook position does not need to judge the nutritional suitability of a therapeutic diet, and this occupation is not responsible for dish technique and large-scale cooking.

If you prefer kitchen output and production technique, you can choose the institutional and cafeteria cook direction; if you would rather face patients and recording and verification work, this occupation is more suitable. The two need close handover between the making and the verification of arrangement of therapeutic diets.
Food service managers (11-9051.00)

The level of responsibility differs: food service managers are responsible for the overall management of operating plans, purchasing and inventory, staff scheduling and cost and hygiene compliance; this occupation is responsible for nutrition and catering-related execution and records and accepts professional supervision by the dietitian. A management position is responsible for cost and staff but does not bear the recording and execution responsibility of nutrition care.

If you want to take on operations and staff management and hold cost and compliance responsibility, you can choose the food service manager direction; if you want to stay in the specific steps of nutrition care and build clinical and group catering experience, this occupation is closer. The two connect on menus and cost calculation (this occupation also takes part in cost calculation and new product testing).
Nursing assistants (31-1131.00)

The care content differs: nursing assistants are responsible for patients' daily living care, positioning and transfer, some feeding assistance and basic vital sign observation; this occupation is responsible for recording and verification in the nutrition and catering execution steps, meal arrangement and distribution, and nutrition teaching. Both work at the bedside, but one focuses on daily care and the other on nutrition and catering execution, with different professional judgments and record content.

If you would rather do bedside care and help patients with daily living, you can choose the nursing assistant direction; if you would rather work in the nutrition and food service steps and bear recording and verification responsibility, this occupation fits better. The two need to cooperate on feeding assistance and intake records to avoid the same information being duplicated or missed.
Food preparation workers (35-2021.00)

The task scope differs: food preparation workers complete operational tasks such as washing, cutting, portioning and plating according to instructions and are less involved in judging and recording therapeutic diet categories; in addition to arrangement and distribution, this occupation also takes on intake and weight monitoring, dietary history collection, screening assistance, recipe analysis, cost calculation and teaching, which require judgment and documentation.

If you want to enter the food service setting quickly and do operational work, you can start in food preparation and catering positions; if you want to build professional experience in nutrition and catering execution and recording, you should aim for a position in this occupation and learn under the supervision of a dietitian.
Medical assistants (31-9092.00)

The work setting and tasks differ: medical assistants in outpatient or clinic settings take on appointments, data entry, measuring vital signs and assisting with examinations and other administrative and clinical support work; the work object of this occupation is the nutrition and catering execution steps, including therapeutic diet verification, meal arrangement and distribution, sample retention and disinfection records and nutrition teaching. Both centre on process and records, but the content and the specifications they belong to differ.

If you prefer outpatient processes and patient reception and documentation support, you can choose the medical assistant direction; if you are more interested in nutrition and catering execution and food safety, this occupation is more suitable. The two can transfer to each other, but the respective care specifications and recording requirements must be learned anew.

The object of a fit judgment is the work itself, not a personality label. Every day this occupation involves recording intake and weight truthfully by meal, verifying therapeutic diets against the ordered category, repeatedly verifying and documenting during catering and distribution, and communicating continuously with patients and families as well as nursing and catering colleagues. First consider whether you are willing to do these tasks and can accept such conditions, and then see whether the personality description fits.

First group of signals: whether you can stay meticulous in repetitive recording and verification — intake, weight, portions, temperature and sample retention times must all be registered item by item, and one omitted record may leave the dietitian with incomplete information.

Second group of signals: acceptance of communication and service — continuous contact with others is required (78%), face-to-face discussion every day (79%), and you must face both the questions and emotions of patients and families and repeatedly confirm with nursing and catering colleagues, and accept executing and explaining a plan determined by someone else (the dietitian).

Third group of signals: ability to carry out hygiene and infection control requirements — exposure to disease or infection every day (82%) means putting on and taking off protective equipment and hand hygiene are hard requirements; they cannot be omitted because you are busy or find it troublesome.

Fourth group of signals: clarity about the boundaries of responsibility — knowing what is execution and recording and what must be left to the dietitian or physician; being willing to ask when uncertain, and not exceeding authority to give a treatment plan in order to help the patient.

Fifth group of signals: adaptation to time and pace — catering and mealtimes are concentrated, time pressure is 61% every day, and you need to complete verification and distribution according to the process at peak times and accept early shifts or shift work.

Sixth group of signals: how you learn and collaborate — you need to learn recipe and nutrition basics, food safety and sample retention and disinfection standards, and the operation of nutrition analysis and medical information systems, and to express accurately what you know in interdisciplinary meetings.

Seventh group of signals: emotion and tolerance — patience and restraint are needed with long-term care patients, anxious families or refusal to eat; a relatively stable willingness to invest is also needed for repetitive work and contributions that are not always visible.

entries.answer: A typical day revolves around meals and records: observe and record the patient's intake and eating method by meal, measure and register weight according to procedure, and organise changes, progress and dietary problems before reporting to the dietitian; collect and assess dietary history and assist with nutrition screening and assessment; prepare meals by calculating against recipes and portions, and verify the arrangement and recipients of therapeutic diets and special meals against the ordered diet category and allergy and swallowing restrictions; implement sample retention, tableware disinfection, temperature verification and ingredient file records; explain food selection and preparation points to patients and families according to the plan determined by the dietitian, take part in interdisciplinary meetings with other medical professionals, and help refer patients when necessary. The work is mainly in controlled indoor settings and requires wearing protective equipment according to institutional rules and carrying out hand hygiene.
entries.question: What is the specific daily work?

entries.answer: This occupation is the execution and support level in the nutrition and dietetics field: it works under the supervision of a registered dietitian and is responsible for records, organising screening material, meal arrangement and verification, teaching assistance and food safety records. Dietitians and nutritionists are responsible for nutrition assessment and diagnosis and for formulating nutrition therapy plans; nursing staff are responsible for patients' daily care and some feeding assistance; catering and kitchen staff are responsible for bulk production and serving. Under the mainland China scope, nutrition technical personnel with clinical nutrition professional education or training may carry out nutrition consultation, nutrition screening and assessment, enteral nutrition preparation, medical diet arrangement and nutrition teaching, while nutrition diagnosis and nutrition therapy are undertaken by physicians trained in clinical nutrition. The division of labour follows institutional rules and position authorization.
entries.question: How is the division of labour with dietitians and nursing and catering colleagues arranged?

details: Chinese medical institutions: Article 5 of the 2022 guideline provides that physicians trained in clinical nutrition carry out diagnosis and treatment as required, and Article 6 provides that nutrition technical personnel with professional education or training carry out consultation, screening and assessment, enteral nutrition preparation, medical diet arrangement and teaching as required, and this is not uniformly reduced to merely organising material. Article 5 of the annex requires nutrition screening to be completed by medical staff with the relevant practice qualification and training, with the first-visit physician as the first responsible person; Article 10 provides that assessment is carried out by clinical nutrition technical personnel collecting clinical data, and Article 14 provides that records are included in the medical record. Pre-job training or a public nutritionist certificate does not itself replace the relevant practice qualification. Article 8 of the guideline requires the medical diet and enteral nutrition preparation departments of a clinical nutrition department to establish staff health files, ingredient files, tableware disinfection, food sample retention and hygiene inspection systems, and this is not interpreted directly as the same clinical duty for every school canteen or every cook; specific temperature, two-person verification and shutdown and recovery are verified against the applicable procedures, and no uniform parameters were obtained in this round.

subject.summary: Dietetic technicians (United States side O*NET-SOC 29-2051.00) are an execution and support position that assists in providing food service and nutrition programmes under the supervision of a registered dietitian: observing and recording the patient's intake and weight changes and reporting changes, progress and dietary problems to the dietitian; collecting and assessing the individual's dietary history in order to carry out nutrition assessment and assisting in formulating nutrition plans; preparing main meals according to recipes and calculating group portions, planning menus and meals according to nutritional needs and established guidelines, or guiding individuals and families on food selection, preparation and menu planning; supervising food production and service, or assisting the dietitian with food service supervision and planning; analyzing and standardising menus and recipes and testing new products, calculating food and beverage costs and assisting with cost control; recording and verifying the arrangement and distribution of therapeutic diets and special meals and tracking food safety and sample retention and tableware disinfection requirements; taking part in interdisciplinary meetings with other medical professionals, assisting the dietitian in researching food, nutrition and food service systems, organising induction and in-service education, referring patients to other related services to maintain continuity of care, and giving dietary and nutrition health presentations to populations. United States scope: in the May 2025 wage data for this occupation the median annual wage is 37,640 USD (median hourly 18.09 USD), with annual percentiles of 29,720 / 33,880 / 37,640 / 45,750 / 54,020 USD (hourly percentiles 14.29 / 16.29 / 18.09 / 22.00 / 25.97); the O*NET summary page gives 2024 employment of about 30,900 people, growth of 3% to 4% over 2024—2034 (average) and about 4,000 projected job openings, with the main industry being healthcare and social assistance; the preparation level is Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), usually requiring 1—2 years of training, with apprenticeship opportunities, and among new hire feedback 35% consider an associate degree or other two-year degree necessary and 27% consider a postsecondary certificate necessary; the interest code is SCR; the work context includes continuous contact with others 78%, being indoors in a controlled environment 91% every day, face-to-face discussion 79% every day, exposure to disease or infection 82% every day, time pressure 61% every day, and wearing common protective equipment 65% every day. Mainland China scope: nutrition and dietary execution work in hospital clinical nutrition departments and group catering is carried out by nutrition technical personnel with clinical nutrition professional education or training, who may carry out nutrition consultation, nutrition screening and assessment, enteral nutrition preparation, medical diet arrangement and nutrition teaching, but this is not physician practice and does not involve nutrition diagnosis and treatment; the public nutritionist has changed to occupational skill level recognition and the certificate does not carry physician practice qualification. Public statistics have not published occupational-level wages corresponding to this occupation, and this page retains the gap as it stands.
